note: When merging onto an interstate, use the entrance ramp and acceleration lane to reach the speed of traffic, check your mirrors and blind spots, signal, and find a safe gap before merging. Do not expect others to yield for you, and do not stop at the end of the ramp unless traffic or signs require it.

question: If you parallel park facing downhill, how should you turn your wheels?
options: a:Turn your wheels away from the side of the road.,b:Keep your wheels straight.,c:Turn your wheels sharply toward the side of the road.
note: When parking facing downhill, turn your front wheels toward the curb or road edge. If the vehicle starts to roll, the front tire will roll into the curb or edge and help stop the car from moving into traffic.

question: Driving while impaired by medication is allowed:
options: a:Only on short trips.,b:If you feel alert enough.,c:Under no circumstances.,d:If your doctor prescribed it.
note: Driving under the influence of anything that impairs you—including prescription or over‑the‑counter medication—is illegal. Even if a doctor prescribed it or you feel okay, you must not drive if the drug affects your judgment, reaction time, coordination, or alertness.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: If your view at an intersection is blocked to the side, what should you do?
options: a:Slow down or stop as needed, then inch forward until you can see clearly.,b:Maintain your speed and look both ways.,c:Stop well before the intersection and proceed without inching forward.
note: When your view is blocked at an intersection, you must slow or stop as needed, then move forward gradually until you can see clearly in both directions. Do not enter the cross traffic lane until you are sure it is safe. In many situations this will mean coming to a complete stop first, then inching forward to improve your view.

question: To reduce the risk of hydroplaning in heavy rain you should:
options: a:Move to the shoulder immediately.,b:Use cruise control to maintain steady speed.,c:Decrease your speed.,d:Shift into neutral while driving through water.
note: Hydroplaning happens when your tires ride on a layer of water and lose contact with the road. The best way to reduce this risk is to slow down in heavy rain, especially when water is pooling on the road. Avoid sudden steering or braking and do not use cruise control in heavy rain.

question: Why should you leave extra space in front of a large truck?
options: a:So you can use the space to stop quickly.,b:Because trucks require more distance to stop.,c:To reduce the truck's fuel consumption.,d:To allow the truck to pull off the road.
note: Large trucks are much heavier than passenger cars and need a longer distance to stop. Leaving extra space in front of a truck gives the truck driver more room to slow or stop and gives you time to react if traffic changes suddenly.

question: An orange and red triangular emblem displayed on the back of a vehicle means:
options: a:The vehicle has the right-of-way.,b:The vehicle is an emergency vehicle.,c:There is roadwork ahead.,d:The vehicle is a slow-moving vehicle.
note: An orange and red triangular emblem on the back of a vehicle is a slow‑moving vehicle sign. It warns that the vehicle usually travels at 25 mph or less, such as farm equipment or animal‑drawn vehicles, so you should be prepared to slow down and pass only when safe and legal.

question: Which is a dangerous habit when driving in work zones?
options: a:Tailgating another vehicle.,b:Failing to carefully watch for workers and moving equipment.,c:Both tailgating another vehicle and failing to watch for workers and equipment.
note: In work zones you must slow down, increase following distance, and watch carefully for workers, equipment, and changing traffic patterns. Tailgating reduces your time to react if traffic suddenly stops, and not watching for workers or machinery can lead to serious crashes. Both behaviors are dangerous and must be avoided.

question: If pedestrians are illegally crossing in the middle of the street, you:
options: a:Should honk and proceed.,b:Do not have to stop for them.,c:May drive around them aggressively.,d:Must still yield and stop for them.
note: Drivers must always exercise due care to avoid hitting pedestrians, even when pedestrians are crossing illegally. You must slow or stop if necessary to prevent a collision and should not honk aggressively or try to drive around them in a way that could endanger them.

question: You should leave extra following distance when you are behind:
options: a:Motor vehicles.,b:Station wagons.,c:Motorcycles.,d:Tractors only.
note: Motorcycles are smaller and harder to see, and they can stop or swerve more quickly than larger vehicles. Leave extra following distance so you have more time to react if the motorcyclist slows, stops, or swerves to avoid road hazards.

question: Why is driving at night more dangerous than daytime driving?
options: a:Your vehicle handles worse at night.,b:Roads are always more slippery at night.,c:Traffic laws are different at night.,d:You cannot see as far ahead at night.
note: At night your visibility is reduced because you must rely on headlights, and glare from other vehicles can further limit how far ahead you can see. Since you cannot see hazards as early as in daylight, driving at night is more dangerous and requires slower speeds and greater following distance.

question: If you plan to turn left at the next corner, to whom must you yield the right-of-way?
options: a:Pedestrians on the sidewalk waiting for a "Walk" signal.,b:Oncoming vehicles also turning left.,c:All approaching vehicles.
note: When turning left, you must yield to oncoming traffic that is going straight or turning right, and to pedestrians and bicyclists crossing your path. Only turn when there is a safe gap in oncoming traffic and after yielding to any pedestrians in the crosswalk.

question: To avoid loss of traction on wet roads you should:
options: a:Increase following distance only when visibility is low.,b:Slow down.,c:Make abrupt turns.,d:Apply brakes firmly and abruptly.
note: On wet roads, your tires have less grip and can hydroplane. Slowing down reduces the chance of losing traction and gives you more time to react. Avoid sudden steering, hard braking, or rapid acceleration because abrupt movements can cause skids.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When traffic is merging into your lane on a freeway, you should:
options: a:Make room for merging vehicles when it is safe to do so.,b:Assert your right-of-way by speeding up.,c:Always maintain your current exact position.,d:Drive onto the shoulder to let them in.
note: When traffic is merging onto a freeway, you should help the flow of traffic by making room when it is safe. Adjust your speed or change lanes if possible so merging vehicles can enter smoothly. Do not speed up to block them or drive onto the shoulder.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Which action should you never do when changing lanes?
options: a:Check your blind spots by looking over your left or right shoulder.,b:Change lanes or pass within an intersection.,c:Check for other drivers moving into the same lane.
note: You should never change lanes or pass within an intersection because traffic and turning movements are more complex and less predictable there. Always wait until you are past the intersection, then signal, check mirrors, and look over your shoulder to check blind spots before changing lanes.

question: When you see a school crossing sign, what should you do?
options: a:Always stop,b:Always sound your horn when you see children.,c:Be alert for children and be prepared to stop.
note: A school crossing sign warns that children may be crossing the road. You are not required to stop every time you see the sign, but you must slow down if needed, watch carefully for children, and be prepared to stop if they are in or near the crosswalk.

question: When poor weather or light requires using lights, which should you use?
options: a:Use your high beams.,b:Use your parking lights.,c:Use your low beams.
note: In rain, fog, or snow, use low beam headlights so you can see and be seen without causing glare. High beams can reflect off moisture in the air and make it harder for you and other drivers to see. Parking lights alone are not enough for safe visibility while driving.

question: A red, octagon-shaped traffic sign always means:
options: a:Stop.,b:Wrong way.,c:Do not enter.,d:Yield.
note: A red octagon is reserved exclusively for STOP signs in the U.S. When you see this shape and color, you must come to a complete stop at the stop line, crosswalk, or before entering the intersection, and proceed only when it is safe.

question: When encountering a person crossing with a white cane or guide dog, you should:
options: a:Stop and remain stopped until the person is safely clear of your path.,b:Drive slowly around them.,c:Honk to alert them and then proceed.,d:Yell instructions to help them cross.
note: A person using a white cane or guide dog is visually impaired and has the right-of-way. You must stop and remain stopped until the pedestrian has completely crossed and is safely clear of your path. Do not honk, shout, or try to drive around them, as this can confuse or endanger them.

question: Fatigue increases your risk of what?
options: a:Being late for an appointment.,b:Missing an exit.,c:Falling asleep behind the wheel and crashing.
note: Fatigue slows your reactions, reduces your awareness, and can cause you to fall asleep while driving. This greatly increases the risk of a serious or fatal crash, which is why you should rest before driving and take breaks on long trips.

question: You must yield the right-of-way to any pedestrian who is:
options: a:Only in a marked crosswalk.,b:Far from the crosswalk.,c:Standing on the curb.,d:In any crosswalk or intersection.
note: Drivers must yield to pedestrians in both marked and unmarked crosswalks at intersections. Any intersection, whether or not it has painted lines, can contain a legal crosswalk. Always be prepared to stop for pedestrians who are crossing where they have the right-of-way.

question: Which of the following is the only reliable way to lower your blood alcohol concentration (BAC)?
options: a:Taking a cold shower.,b:Eating high-fat foods.,c:Drinking coffee.,d:Time.
note: Only time reduces your blood alcohol concentration. Your body must metabolize the alcohol, and things like coffee, food, or cold showers do not speed this up. If you have been drinking, waiting long enough before driving is the only safe and reliable option.

question: Regulatory traffic signs are typically what color?
options: a:White.,b:Yellow.,c:Green.,d:Blue.
note: Regulatory signs show laws and rules you must obey, such as speed limits, no parking, and turn restrictions. In the U.S., these signs are typically white rectangles or squares with black, red, or green symbols or lettering, which is why white is the correct color choice.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: What is the best thing to do when you become sleepy while driving?
options: a: Increase your speed to get away from other vehicles,b: Move over to the right lane and continue driving,c: Drive to a safe place stop and rest
note: When you start to feel sleepy while driving, your reaction time, judgment, and awareness drop quickly, and rolling down a window or turning up the radio will not keep you safe. The safest action is to get off the road as soon as you can safely do so, park in a safe place, and rest before continuing to drive.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Medications for sleep, anxiety, pain, colds, or allergies.
options: a: May impair your driving,b: May increase the bad effects of alcohol on your driving,c: Both of the above
note: Many prescription and over‑the‑counter medicines, including those for sleep, anxiety, pain, colds, or allergies, can make you drowsy, dizzy, or less alert, which impairs driving. When combined with alcohol, these effects can become much stronger and more dangerous, greatly increasing your risk of a crash.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You shouldn’t drive.
options: a: After you have taken any drink drug or medication which changes how you think or act or causes you to be less careful,b: If you are not alert,c: Both of the above
note: You must not drive if you are under the influence of anything that changes how you think, react, or behave, including alcohol, drugs, or certain medications. You also must be fully alert so you can notice hazards and react quickly. If either condition is true—impaired by substances or not alert—you should not drive, so “both of the above” is correct.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: About drugs and driving, what statement is correct?
options: a: Even over-the-counter drugs can impair your driving,b: Any prescription drug is safe to use if you don’t feel drowsy,c: Only illegal drugs can impair your driving
note: Many prescription and over‑the‑counter medicines can slow your reactions, make you sleepy, or otherwise affect your driving, even if they are legal and properly used. Illegal drugs can also impair driving, but they are not the only concern. Because even non‑prescription drugs can affect your ability to drive safely, the correct statement is that over‑the‑counter drugs can impair your driving.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: On a long trip how can you prevent fatigue?
options: a: Get enough sleep before the trip,b: Plan to drive long trips with a companion,c: All of the above
note: To prevent fatigue on a long trip, you should prepare before you drive and manage your trip while you are driving. Getting enough sleep beforehand helps you start the trip rested, and planning to drive with a companion allows you to share driving, stay more alert, and have someone who can notice signs of drowsiness. Using both strategies together is the safest approach, so all of the listed actions help prevent fatigue.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Who is most at risk?
options: a: Drivers who are fatigued or drowsy,b: Drivers who are driving on long, monotonous roads,c: All of the above
note: Drivers who are already tired and drivers traveling on long, monotonous roads are both at high risk for drowsy driving. Fatigue slows your reaction time, narrows your attention, and can cause you to fall asleep at the wheel. Long, boring stretches of road make it easier to lose focus and become sleepy, especially if you were already tired. Because both groups are at increased risk, all of the above is correct.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Fatigue results in an increased risk of:
options: a: Missing an exit.,b: Being late for an appointment.,c: Falling asleep behind the wheel and crashing.
note: Fatigue and drowsiness make you less alert, slow your reaction time, and can cause you to fall asleep at the wheel. This greatly increases the risk of a serious crash, including running off the road or into other vehicles. While you might also miss an exit or be late, the major safety risk is falling asleep and crashing.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: What should you do if you feel fatigued while driving?
options: a: Increase your speed to reach your destination more quickly.,b: Increase the volume of your radio.,c: Find a safe parking area to take a short nap.
note: Fatigue and drowsiness can affect your vision and increase reaction time to hazards. 'Find a safe parking area to take a short nap.' is the only option that directly addresses the issue of fatigue.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: What should you do if you have an argument with another person and you are angry?
options: a: Loudly play the radio while driving so you won’t think about your argument.,b: Take a few minutes to cool off before driving.,c: Drive on the interstate to let off steam.
note: Strong emotions like anger, stress, or frustration can distract you and cause you to take risks or misjudge situations on the road. If you have had an argument and feel angry, it is safer to wait and take a few minutes to calm down before driving so you can focus fully on the road.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Reaction time slows after:
options: a: Drinking alcohol.,b: Sleeping.,c: Working hard.
note: Alcohol is a depressant that slows brain function and reaction time, making it harder to respond quickly to hazards. Even small amounts of alcohol can impair your ability to judge distances, react to sudden changes, and control your vehicle safely.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: To turn quickly, your hands must be:
options: a: On opposite sides of the steering wheel.,b: Next to each other on the top of the steering wheel.,c: On the top and bottom of the steering wheel.
note: To make quick, controlled turns, your hands should be on opposite sides of the steering wheel, typically around the 9-and-3 or 8-and-4 positions. This gives you maximum leverage and control and allows you to use proper hand‑to‑hand (push‑pull) steering without crossing your arms.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: While drinking alcohol, what is a potential effect of taking a prescription drug?
options: a: There will likely be no effect.,b: It will make you more alert.,c: It can make you unfit to drive.
note: Combining alcohol with prescription drugs can greatly increase drowsiness, slow your reactions, and affect judgment. Even medications that are safe alone can make you unfit to drive when mixed with alcohol, so you must assume your driving ability can be impaired.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Which one of these statements is correct?
options: a: Use your left foot to brake.,b: Use your right foot for both braking and accelerating your vehicle.,c: You should always brake abruptly to ensure stopping.
note: In normal passenger vehicles with automatic or manual transmissions, you should use your right foot for both the accelerator and the brake. This helps prevent pressing both pedals by mistake and gives you consistent control. The left foot is reserved for the clutch in manual‑transmission vehicles, not for braking.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You should use your turn signals when parking next to a curb
options: a: When pulling next to or away from the curb,b: When pulling next to but not away from the curb,c: Only when pulling away from the curb
note: You must signal any time you change your vehicle’s position in traffic, including when you pull in toward the curb to park and when you pull away from the curb to re-enter traffic. Signaling lets other drivers and cyclists anticipate your movement and adjust safely.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You should use your turn signals in time to let other drivers see your intentions.
options: a: Before you move,b: After you move,c: Only when it’s raining
note: Turn signals must be activated before you start moving, turning, or changing lanes so others have time to see and react to your intentions. Signaling after you move defeats the purpose and increases the risk of a collision.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You should signal at least 100 feet before turning.
options: a: Before every lane change.,b: At least 5 seconds before you change lanes on a freeway.,c: None of the above.,d: both a and b
note: You should signal well in advance of any change in direction or lane position. That includes signaling before every lane change and for at least five seconds before changing lanes on a freeway, as well as at least 100 feet before turning. This gives other drivers time to see and respond to your actions.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Use your turn signals.
options: a: When changing lanes or merging into traffic.,b: When turning left or right.,c: Both of the above.,d: None of the above
note: Use your turn signals whenever you intend to change where your vehicle is going in the roadway, including turning left or right and changing lanes or merging. Signaling clearly communicates your intentions and helps prevent crashes.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: What happens when you do not signal when required?
options: a: You may get a ticket,b: You may cause an accident,c: All of the above
note: Failing to signal when required can lead to a traffic citation and also increases the chance of a collision because other road users are not warned about your next move. Proper signaling is both a legal requirement and a key safety practice.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: What should bicyclists do to signal a turn?
options: a: Using their vehicle's signal lights,b: Using hand and arm positions,c: Using their horn
note: Bicyclists do not have electric turn signals like cars, so they must use hand and arm signals. To indicate a turn, a bicyclist extends an arm in the direction of the turn so others can clearly see where they intend to go.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When pulling away from the curb do you need to signal?
options: a: Yes. You need to signal when you pull away from the curb,b: No you only need to signal when you approach the curb,c: only if there are other vehicles around you
note: You must always signal before pulling away from the curb so other drivers, bicyclists, and pedestrians know you are about to enter the traffic lane. Signaling is required even if you think no one is around, because traffic can appear quickly.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Before changing lanes, when is it required to signal?
options: a: At all times,b: Only when there are other vehicles nearby,c: Only when changing lanes on a freeway
note: You are required to signal every time you change lanes, regardless of speed or traffic conditions. Signaling gives other road users time to react and helps prevent collisions, even if you do not see anyone nearby.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Is it legal to use horn in residential areas?
options: a: Yes, as long as you use it only when necessary for safety,b: It is only legal if you live in the residential area,c: No it is not legal to use the horn in residential areas unless it is an emergency
note: You may legally use your horn in residential areas when it is necessary for safety, such as to avoid a collision or warn others of a hazard. You should not use the horn unnecessarily or just to make noise, but it is allowed whenever it helps prevent danger.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: While making a turn you should signal continuously because
options: a: It is illegal to turn off your signal before completing a turn.,b: It lets other drivers know what your intentions are.,c: It is always unsafe to turn off a signal before completing a turn.
note: You must keep your turn signal on throughout the entire turn so other road users clearly understand what you plan to do. Signaling continuously before and during the turn gives drivers, cyclists, and pedestrians time to react and adjust their speed or position, which helps prevent collisions.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: To reduce road rage what can you do?
options: a: Always signal your intention when changing lanes.,b: Talk on your cell phone while driving.,c: Use your horn frequently.
note: Signaling before changing lanes or turning helps other drivers anticipate your movements and reduces surprises that can trigger anger or aggressive driving. Clear, early communication with turn signals is one of the simplest ways to prevent misunderstandings and lower the risk of road rage.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You can use your horn when:
options: a: Another vehicle is in your way.,b: It may help prevent a collision.,c: Another driver makes a mistake.
note: Use your horn only when it may help prevent a collision or to alert others to a hazard. The horn is a safety device, not a way to express frustration. Honking just because someone is in your way or makes a mistake can escalate tension and is often unsafe or illegal.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When a vehicle is approaching towards you, before how many feet should you switch from high beam to low beam headlights?
options: a: 900 feet.,b: 700 feet.,c: 500 feet.
note: When another vehicle is approaching you at night, you must dim your high beams to low beams within about 500 feet. This prevents you from blinding the oncoming driver, helping them see the road and stay in their lane, which reduces the risk of a head‑on collision.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: If a driver is having trouble seeing other vehicles because of dust or smoke which lights should be used?
options: a: Parking lights.,b: Emergency lights.,c: Headlights.
note: In dust, smoke, or similar low‑visibility conditions, you should turn on your headlights so other drivers can see you more easily. Using headlights (not just parking or emergency lights) improves your visibility to others and helps prevent collisions in poor conditions.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Turn on your headlights
options: a: Only when it is completely dark outside.,b: When it is too dark to see from 1000 feet away.,c: When it is too dark to see from 500 feet away.,d: None of the above
note: Headlights are required whenever it is too dark to see people or vehicles clearly from about 1,000 feet away. Turning them on early improves your visibility and makes it easier for others to see you.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You can drive using only your parking lights:
options: a: 30 minutes after sunset or 30 minutes before sunrise,b: on foggy days,c: Not under any circumstances
note: Parking lights alone are not bright enough for safe driving and do not meet legal lighting requirements. You must use your headlights when driving in low‑visibility conditions; parking lights are only for when the vehicle is stopped or parked.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When driving at night on a poorly lit street and using high beams, reduce your lights intensity within 500 feet of:
options: a: a vehicle approaching you from behind,b: an oncoming vehicle,c: a sharp curve or hill
note: High beams can temporarily blind oncoming drivers. You must dim your high beams to low beams within about 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle so both drivers can see the road safely.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When should you be tuning off your turn signals?
options: a: As soon as you have completed the turn or lane change,b: As soon as you begin the turn or lane change,c: Before you begin the turn or lane change
note: Turn signals are used to warn others of your intention to turn or change lanes. Once you have completed the maneuver and no longer need to communicate it, you should turn off your signal so other drivers are not misled.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When is it necessary to use your headlights while driving on mountain roads and in tunnels?
options: a: Only on cloudy days,b: Only at night,c: Always regardless of weather conditions
note: Headlights should be used on mountain roads and in tunnels even on sunny days so other drivers can see you clearly as light conditions change quickly. This improves visibility for you and makes your vehicle more visible to others.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Signal your intentions with your brake lights or hazard lights when you:
options: a: Need to warn other drivers of an accident or hazard ahead.,b: Are temporarily stopped in a traffic lane for an emergency.,c: Are backing out of a parking space.
note: When you see a collision or hazard ahead, you should warn drivers behind you by lightly tapping your brakes or turning on your hazard lights. This gives following drivers extra time to slow down and helps prevent rear-end collisions.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Visibility can be poor during dawn, dusk or in rain or snow. To let other drivers of your presence, you should turn:
options: a: Up the instrument panel lights.,b: On your parking lights.,c: On your headlights.
note: During dawn, dusk, rain, or snow, your visibility and other drivers’ ability to see you are reduced. You should turn on your low‑beam headlights so you can see the road better and so other drivers can see your vehicle from a safe distance.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Use low beams when approaching another vehicle or when following within 300 feet of a vehicle
options: a: That you are following within about 300 feet.,b: Approaching you from the opposite direction.,c: That is more than 300 feet ahead of you.
note: High beams can blind drivers ahead of you. You must switch to low beams when you are within about 300 feet of a vehicle you are following so you do not shine bright lights into their mirrors and impair their vision.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When visibility is reduced due to rain, snow, or fog, activate your windshield wipers and use your headlights:
options: a: On the high beam setting.,b: So other drivers can see you.,c: Only when driving on the freeway.
note: In rain, snow, or fog, you must turn on your low‑beam headlights whenever you need to use your windshield wipers. The main purpose is to make your vehicle easier for others to see, not to see farther with high beams, which can reflect off moisture and reduce visibility.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: To be more visible as dusk approaches, you should use your:
options: a: Parking lights.,b: Low beam headlights.,c: Emergency flashers.
note: Use your low beam headlights as dusk approaches so others can see you and you can see the road. Parking lights and emergency flashers are not meant for normal driving visibility.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: If visibility is poor due to fog, rain, or snow, utilize:
options: a: Low beams.,b: High beams.,c: Fog lights together with low beams.
note: In fog, rain, or snow, always use low beam headlights. High beams reflect off moisture in the air and can cause glare, making it harder to see. If your vehicle has fog lights, you may use them together with low beams, but not by themselves.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Avoid using your horn.
options: a: When visibility ahead is limited.,b: If you might hit another vehicle.,c: Near blind pedestrians.
note: Use your horn to help avoid collisions, such as when another driver may not see you and a crash is possible. Do not use your horn near blind pedestrians, because they rely on sound cues and may be startled or confused by unnecessary honking.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When a vehicle's left and right turn signals are flashing at the same time, it indicates...
options: a: It is carrying children to or from school,b: Let the vehicle have the right-of-way,c: There may be a hazard or an accident ahead
note: When both turn signals flash together, they act as hazard lights. This usually means the vehicle is stopped or moving slowly due to a breakdown, hazard, or collision ahead, so you should be prepared to slow down or change lanes safely.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Drivers are required to, when parking on public roads,...
options: a: Move as far away from traffic as possible,b: Always park on the left side of the roadway,c: Both a and b
note: When you must park or stop on a public road, you should pull as far off the roadway and away from moving traffic as is safely possible. This reduces the chance of being hit by passing vehicles. You do not "always park on the left"; in the U.S. you normally park on the right side, and only where parking is legal and safe.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Feel free to use your horn when driving on tight mountain roads.
options: a: To alert oncoming traffic where you cannot see at least 200 feet ahead,b: To let pedestrians know you are there,c: To signal to other drivers that you are in a hurry
note: On narrow or tight mountain roads where you cannot see at least about 200 feet ahead, you should briefly use your horn to alert oncoming traffic to your presence. The horn is for preventing collisions and warning of hazards, not for hurrying other drivers or routinely signaling pedestrians.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Activate your hazard lights or tap your brake lights if you:
options: a: Need to warn other drivers of a collision ahead.,b: Are temporarily parked in a traffic lane to make delivery.,c: Are backing out of a parking space.
note: If you see a collision or hazard ahead, you should warn drivers behind you by turning on your hazard lights or lightly tapping your brake pedal several times. This gives following drivers extra time to slow down and helps prevent rear-end collisions.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Should you need to park your vehicle outside of designated areas:
options: a: Park with your reverse lights on.,b: Make sure your vehicle is clearly visible to approaching drivers.,c: Park five feet from the curb.
note: If you cannot park in a normal designated area or completely off the road, stop where other drivers can clearly see you and your vehicle from a sufficient distance. Good visibility in all directions gives approaching drivers time to slow down or move over, reducing the risk of a collision.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: If you have a vehicle malfunction?
options: a: Signal and pull into the slow lane.,b: Stop in your lane and put on your hazard lights.,c: Put on your hazard lights and pull off the road.
note: If your vehicle has a problem, you should first turn on your hazard (emergency) flashers to warn other drivers. Then, if you can, steer smoothly and safely off the roadway and stop in a safe place away from traffic. Never stop in a traffic lane unless your vehicle is completely disabled and cannot be moved.

question: It is forbidden to drive over a solid double line in the middle of the road to
options: a: Overtake and pass another vehicle,b: Make a left turn,c: Enter a private driveway
note: Double solid yellow center lines mean you may not drive to the left of the lines to pass another vehicle. However, you may usually cross them to make a left turn or to enter or exit a driveway or side road when it is safe and not otherwise prohibited. Passing another moving vehicle over double solid yellow lines is not allowed.

question: You should treat lines as a barrier when:
options: a: Two sets of solid double white lines are spaced 2 feet apart,b: Two sets of solid double yellow lines are spaced 2 or more feet apart,c: Two sets of broken yellow lines are spaced 1 foot apart
note: When you see two sets of solid double yellow lines separated by 2 or more feet, they are treated as a physical barrier. You must not drive on, over, or across them, and you may not use them for left turns or U‑turns except at clearly marked openings. Treat this area as if it were a raised divider.

question: A solid yellow line on your side of the centerline means:
options: a: Reduce your speed.,b: Traffic light ahead.,c: Do not pass.
note: A solid yellow line on your side of the centerline means no passing. It marks the center of a two‑way road and tells you it is unsafe to cross into the oncoming lane to pass another vehicle.

question: Broken yellow lines are used on streets or highways to:
options: a: Indicate no passing zones.,b: Separate lanes of traffic moving in the same direction.,c: Separate lanes of traffic moving in opposite directions.
note: Broken yellow lines separate lanes of traffic moving in opposite directions on two‑way roads. When the broken yellow line is next to your lane, you may cross it to pass if you can do so safely and without interfering with oncoming traffic.

question: Two sets of solid double yellow lines that are two or more feet apart:
options: a: May be crossed to enter or exit a private driveway.,b: May not be crossed for any reason.,c: Should be treated as a separate traffic lane.
note: Two sets of double solid yellow lines at least two feet apart act as a physical barrier. You must not drive on, over, or across them to turn or make a U‑turn, except at designated openings provided for that purpose.

question: When solid double yellow lines separate the lanes of traffic:
options: a: Passing is permitted from the left.,b: Passing is permitted from the right.,c: Passing is not permitted from either direction.
note: Double solid yellow lines mark a no‑passing zone for traffic in both directions. You may not cross them to pass another vehicle. They act as a barrier between opposing flows of traffic, and you should stay in your lane unless making a permitted left turn into or out of a driveway or side road where allowed by local law.

question: You are allowed to pass a vehicle when:
options: a: You are on a hill or curve.,b: You are on a road with a solid line next to your lane.,c: You are on a road with a broken line next to your lane.
note: A broken yellow center line next to your lane means you may pass another vehicle if it is safe and legal to do so. You must have enough clear distance ahead, no oncoming traffic close by, and no signs or markings prohibiting passing. A solid line next to your lane or limited visibility on hills and curves means you must not pass.

question: What should you do to ensure lane is clear before moving into it?
options: a: Turn your head and look,b: Look in the left side mirror,c: Look into the rear-view mirror
note: Mirrors do not show your blind spots. Before moving into another lane, you must turn your head and look over your shoulder in the direction you want to move. This quick head check lets you see vehicles, motorcycles, or bicycles that may be hidden beside you and helps prevent sideswipe collisions.

question: When turning, drivers must signal continuously for the final 100 feet before the turn. How should a driver signal when changing lanes?
options: a: Signal, check your mirrors, look over your shoulder, then change lanes when it is safe.,b: Look over your shoulder then signal and then change lanes.,c: Change lanes and then signal.,d: None of the above
note: When changing lanes, you should signal first to alert other drivers, then check your mirrors, and finally look over your shoulder to check your blind spot before moving. Do not change lanes and then signal, and do not move immediately after signaling without checking traffic. The correct sequence is: signal, check mirrors, look over your shoulder, then change lanes when it is safe.

question: When operating a vehicle on a road with multiple lanes and traffic traveling in both directions, you must:
options: a: Drive alongside the other vehicles so the drivers can see you.,b: You should drive ahead of or behind the other vehicles.,c: It is safest to drive in the lane next to the center line.
note: On multi‑lane roads with traffic in both directions, it is safer not to drive right alongside other vehicles. Instead, adjust your speed so you are slightly ahead of or behind them. This gives you more space to maneuver, improves your visibility, and reduces the chance of being involved in a side‑by‑side collision.

question: Prior to switching lanes or overtaking another car, it's crucial to:
options: a: Check your blind spots and mirrors.,b: Signal your intention before changing lanes.,c: All of the above.
note: Before changing lanes or passing, you must both signal your intention and check mirrors and blind spots. Signaling lets other drivers anticipate your move, and checking mirrors and blind spots ensures there is actually space and no one is hidden beside you. Doing all of these steps together is what keeps lane changes safe.

question: Changing from one lane to another is done best:
options: a: Quickly and often.,b: When a car is in your blind spot.,c: Gradually and carefully.
note: Lane changes should be smooth, gradual, and carefully planned. You check traffic, signal, and move over steadily when there is enough space. Sudden or frequent lane changes increase the risk of collisions, especially if another vehicle is in your blind spot.

question: Double solid yellow lines indicate that:
options: a: Neither lane may pass.,b: Both lanes may pass.,c: The lane to the right may pass.
note: Double solid yellow lines between lanes of traffic moving in opposite directions mean that neither direction may pass or cross the lines, except to turn left safely into or out of a driveway or side road where allowed. They act as a strong no‑passing barrier. You must stay in your lane and not drive to the left of these lines unless making a permitted left turn or when directed by traffic control.

question: When driving on a highway alongside a single broken white line:
options: a: You cannot cross the line to pass.,b: You may cross the line to pass and change lanes.,c: You may only cross the line to change lanes if you are in the left lane.
note: A single broken white line separates lanes of traffic moving in the same direction. You may cross it to change lanes or pass when it is safe. Always check mirrors, blind spots, and signal before moving across the line.

question: If you drive faster than other vehicles on a road with one lane moving in each direction and continually pass the other cars, you will:
options: a: Get you to your destination much more quickly and safely.,b: Increase your chances of an collision.,c: Help prevent traffic congestion.
note: On a two‑lane road with one lane in each direction, driving faster than the flow and constantly passing other vehicles greatly increases your risk of a collision. Frequent lane changes and speed differences reduce your reaction time and surprise other drivers. It is safer to travel at a reasonable, consistent speed with the flow of traffic while obeying the speed limit.

question: Roads with double solid yellow line markings down the center imply that passing is:
options: a: Allowed from both directions.,b: Allowed only from your direction of travel.,c: Not allowed from either direction.
note: A double solid yellow line in the center of the road means vehicles in both directions are prohibited from crossing the lines to pass. You must stay in your lane and may only cross these lines to turn left into or out of a driveway or side road when it is safe and not otherwise prohibited. Passing another moving vehicle is not allowed from either direction.

question: What factors make a car accident more likely?
options: a: Looking over your shoulder while making lane changes,b: Continuously changing lanes to pass other vehicles,c: Adjusting your rearview mirror before you start driving
note: Continuously changing lanes to pass other vehicles increases the risk of collision. 'Stay in one lane as much as possible. Do not weave in and out of traffic. Last minute lane or direction changes may increase the risk of collisions.'

question: Which of the following driving behavior below poses a safety risk on the highway?
options: a: Slower traffic must keep to the right.,b: Change lanes without signaling.,c: If you miss your exit, continue to the next exit instead of making a sudden or unsafe maneuver.
note: Failing to signal before changing lanes is dangerous because other drivers, motorcyclists, and bicyclists cannot anticipate your movement. On highways and interstates, you must always signal before changing lanes so traffic around you has time to react. Slower traffic keeping right is a safe and often legally required practice, and if you miss your exit you should continue to the next exit rather than making sudden or unsafe maneuvers.

question: What is true regarding lane changes?
options: a: You only need to turn and look over your right shoulder for lane changes to the right or left.,b: Look over your right shoulder for a right lane change and your left shoulder for a left lane change.,c: Vehicles with two outside mirrors do not have blind spots.
note: Before changing lanes, always check your mirrors and then turn your head to look over the shoulder on the side you are moving toward. Looking over your right shoulder checks the right-side blind spot for a right lane change; looking over your left shoulder checks the left-side blind spot for a left lane change. Mirrors alone do not show vehicles in your blind spots.

question: When operating a vehicle on a road marked with a single, broken white line down the center:
options: a: You must stay within your lane, but you may cross the line to change lanes when it is safe.,b: You may cross the centerline to change lanes.,c: You may change lanes only from the left lane.
note: A single broken white line separates lanes of traffic moving in the same direction. You must generally stay within your lane, but you are allowed to cross a broken white line when it is safe to change lanes. Always signal, check mirrors, and check your blind spot before moving into another lane.

question: You are currently in the rightmost lane of a four-lane freeway, and your lane is bordered on the left by thick, broken white lines. This indicates you are driving in:
options: a: The carpool lane and must merge into the next lane.,b: A special lane for slow-moving vehicles.,c: An exit or ending lane that may require you to leave the freeway or merge soon.
note: On many freeways, lanes that are about to end or become exit-only lanes are marked with wide or thick broken white lines on the left side of the lane. If you are in a lane bordered by these large broken white lines, you should be prepared for the lane to exit the freeway or end, and you may need to merge into an adjacent through lane if you do not wish to exit.

question: Diamond-shaped symbols designate carpool lanes. Access to these lanes during the times specified on the signs requires you to...
options: a: Be driving a van or bus,b: Drive at the speed limit or have your lights on,c: Have the minimum number of passengers shown on the signs.
note: Diamond symbols on the pavement mark high-occupancy vehicle (HOV or carpool) lanes. During the posted hours, you may only use these lanes if your vehicle meets the occupancy requirement shown on the signs, such as 2 or 3 people per vehicle, or if you qualify under any listed exceptions. Using the lane without the required number of occupants can result in a citation.

question: You are driving a slow moving vehicle on a winding two-lane highway. You must pull over when it is safe and let other drivers pass when you are followed by
options: a: 3 vehicles,b: 4 vehicles,c: 5 or more vehicles
note: On a two-lane road where passing is unsafe, if you are driving slowly and five or more vehicles are stacked up behind you, you must pull into a turnout or safe area when possible and let them pass. This helps prevent unsafe passing and reduces driver frustration.

question: How do you make a right turn at the next intersection?
options: a: Merge into the bicycle lane before making the turn.,b: Wait until the bicycle lane ends then make the turn.,c: Make the turn from your current lane and do not enter the bicycle lane.
note: To make a right turn where there is a bicycle lane, you should safely merge into the bike lane within about 200 feet of the intersection, after checking mirrors and blind spots and yielding to bicyclists. Then complete your right turn from that position near the right edge of the roadway.

question: When a truck or bus is turning right at the same time you are, you should:
options: a: Quickly turn before the truck or bus is able to.,b: Wait until the truck or bus turns before you turn.,c: Squeeze between the truck or bus and the curb.
note: Large trucks and buses need extra space to turn right and often swing wide or start from a lane away from the curb. Never try to pass or squeeze between a turning truck/bus and the curb, and do not try to beat them through the turn. Wait until the truck or bus has completed the turn and the path is clear, then make your turn safely.

question: You are getting ready to make a right turn. You should:
options: a: Signal and turn immediately.,b: Stop before entering the right lane and let all other traffic go first.,c: Slow down or stop
note: When preparing for a right turn, you should slow down in advance so you can turn safely and smoothly. Signal about 100 feet before the turn, move close to the right edge or into the right‑turn lane if there is one, check mirrors and your right blind spot, and be prepared to stop at a limit line, crosswalk, or before entering the intersection if required by a stop sign or red light.

question: You want to make a right turn at an upcoming intersection. You should slow down and:
options: a: Move toward the left side of your lane.,b: Avoid driving in the bicycle lane.,c: Signal for 100 feet before turning.
note: Before making a right turn, you should begin signaling well in advance—about 100 feet in most urban areas—so other drivers, cyclists, and pedestrians know your intentions. As you slow for the turn, stay close to the right edge, check mirrors and your right blind spot, and yield to pedestrians and bicyclists in the crosswalk or bike lane.

question: When turning left from a one-way street onto another one-way street, you must:
options: a: Move into the left lane or to the left side of a single lane.,b: Move into the right lane or to the right side of a single lane.,c: Move into the right lane or to the left side of a single lane.
note: When turning left from a one‑way street onto another one‑way street, you should start from the far‑left lane and enter the left lane on the new street, unless signs or lane markings direct otherwise. Staying in the left lane for a left‑to‑left turn keeps traffic organized and reduces conflicts with vehicles going straight or turning right.

question: When preparing to make a left turn from a two-way street, you should drive:
options: a: Near the right-hand side of the road.,b: Near the centerline.,c: On the left of the centerline.
note: On a two‑way street, you prepare for a left turn by moving as close as is safe to the centerline (or into a marked left‑turn lane). This positions you correctly for the turn and keeps the right lane open for through traffic and right‑turning vehicles.

question: When completing a right turn, which lane is the appropriate one to finish in?
options: a: Any lane free of traffic.,b: The lane closest to the left edge of the road.,c: The lane closest to the right edge of the road.
note: To make a right turn, you should end your turn in the lane closest to the right edge of the road. 'Do not swing wide into another lane of traffic.'

question: While a left turn at an intersection is allowed from either of two lanes, a U-turn is permitted from
options: a: Either of the two lanes,b: Only the left lane,c: Any lane that is open
note: A U‑turn is made from the far‑left position because you are turning across oncoming lanes and need the widest turning radius. Use the left‑turn lane or the far‑left lane only, and never start a U‑turn from a center or right lane unless specific signs or markings direct you to do so.

question: To turn right onto a two-way street from another two-way street, begin in the right-hand lane and end in:
options: a: Any lane that is available,b: The left lane,c: The lane closest to the curb
note: When turning right from a two‑way street onto another two‑way street, start in the right‑hand lane and end in the lane closest to the right curb. Do not swing wide into the left lane; staying in the right lane keeps you out of the path of vehicles that may be turning left or going straight in the other lanes.

question: Left turns on red are allowed from:
options: a: From a one-way street onto a two-way street.,b: From a one-way street onto another one-way street.,c: From a two-way street onto a one-way street.
note: In most U.S. states that allow left turns on red, you may turn left on red only from a one‑way street onto another one‑way street, after stopping and yielding to traffic and pedestrians. Left turns on red from or onto two‑way streets are generally not allowed unless specifically signed.

question: U-turns are prohibited:
options: a: In a parking lot.,b: On or near any curve or hill.,c: On a straight roadway with a clear view for 500 feet in both directions.
note: You must not make a U‑turn where you cannot see far enough ahead to do it safely. On or near a curve or hill, your view of oncoming traffic is limited, so a U‑turn there is prohibited because approaching drivers may not see you in time to react.

question: You should never make a U-turn.
options: a: In residential districts.,b: At or on a railroad crossing.,c: Where there isn't a ‘No U-turn’ sign posted.
note: You must never make a U‑turn at or on a railroad crossing. Trains cannot stop quickly, and tracks must be kept clear at all times. Even if there is no train in sight, using the crossing area to turn around is unsafe and illegal.

question: U-turns in business districts are:
options: a: Always illegal anywhere in a business district.,b: Legal anywhere in a business district if oncoming vehicles are not a hazard.,c: Legal only at intersections in a business district when not otherwise prohibited and when safe.
note: In many states, U‑turns in business districts are allowed only at intersections, and only when there is no sign prohibiting them and it is safe. Making a U‑turn mid‑block in a business district is typically illegal because of frequent driveways, heavy traffic, and limited space.

question: When on a one-way street, a left turn onto another one-way street is permitted only if:
options: a: You increase your speed before the turn.,b: Traffic on the street moves to the right.,c: Traffic on the street moves to the left.
note: When turning left from a one‑way street onto another one‑way street, you may turn into the left‑moving traffic lanes, including on a red light where permitted, after stopping and yielding. This is only allowed when the street you are turning onto carries traffic to the left and there is no sign prohibiting the turn.

question: You are permitted to turn left on a red light only from a:
options: a: One-way street onto a two-way street.,b: One-way street onto a one-way street.,c: Two-way street onto a one-way street.
note: In most U.S. states that allow left turns on red, you may only do so when turning from a one-way street onto another one-way street, after stopping and yielding to traffic, pedestrians, and bicyclists with a green light. Always check for signs that prohibit the turn.

question: When making a left turn from a one-way street onto another one-way street, where should your vehicle be positioned at the start of the turn?
options: a: The lane closest to the center of the street.,b: The far-left lane.,c: You can turn from any lane.
note: When turning left from a one-way street onto another one-way street, position your vehicle in the far-left lane before the turn. This lane is closest to the left curb and gives you the correct angle to enter the new street safely and predictably.

question: To turn left from a one-way street with multiple lanes onto a two-way street, start the turn in:
options: a: The far left lane.,b: Any available lane.,c: The lane closest to the middle of the street.
note: When turning left from a one-way street with multiple lanes onto a two-way street, start from the far-left lane. This lane is closest to the left curb and lines you up properly to enter the correct lane on the two-way street while minimizing conflict with other traffic.

question: When making a left turn from a two-way road onto a one-way road, you must:
options: a: Turn into any lane.,b: Turn into first lane.,c: Turn into second lane.
note: When turning left from a two-way road onto a one-way road, you must turn into the first available lane on the one-way street, usually the lane closest to the left curb. Entering the first lane keeps traffic organized and prevents you from cutting across other lanes where vehicles may be traveling.

question: Upon entering a freeway from an on-ramp and merging, your speed should be driving at:
options: a: The legal speed limit on the freeway,b: About the same speed as the freeway traffic,c: About 10 m.p.h. slower than the freeway speed limit
note: When merging onto a freeway, use the on‑ramp to accelerate to about the same speed as vehicles already on the freeway. Being near the speed of traffic allows you to merge smoothly and safely, as long as you do not exceed the posted speed limit.

question: If you are exiting a parking lot, you...
options: a: Must turn either left or right only when it is safe,b: Have the right-of-way,c: Must yield to traffic and pedestrians before re-entering the road
note: When exiting a parking lot or driveway, you must yield to all traffic already on the road and to pedestrians on the sidewalk or crossing the driveway. Do not assume you have the right‑of‑way; wait until there is a safe gap before entering the roadway.

question: A vehicle that enters a road from a driveway:
options: a: Has the right-of-way,b: Must stop if needed and yield the right-of-way to traffic on the roadway and to pedestrians,c: Must yield only to traffic approaching from the right
note: A driver entering a road from a driveway, alley, or parking lot must stop if necessary and yield to all vehicles already on the roadway and to pedestrians on the sidewalk or crossing the driveway. Traffic already on the road has the right‑of‑way in this situation.

question: You are driving on the freeway and need to exit. You should:
options: a: Use your turn signal, check traffic, and move safely into the exit lane in advance of your exit.,b: Exit immediately without signaling if you see your exit at the last moment.,c: Accelerate sharply into the exit lane to avoid missing your exit.,d: None of the above
note: To exit a freeway safely, you should plan ahead, signal, and move into the exit lane when it is safe. Signal and check mirrors and blind spots as you change lanes one at a time. Once in the proper lane, maintain a safe speed and continue signaling as you approach and take the exit. Never exit suddenly or without signaling.

question: You missed your exit on the freeway. You should not:
options: a: Continue on the freeway and find an alternate route to your destination.,b: Proceed to the next exit.,c: Back up on the road or shoulder.
note: If you miss your freeway exit, you must never back up on the freeway or on the shoulder because it is extremely dangerous and illegal. Instead, continue to the next exit or follow the freeway until you can safely leave and re-route to your destination.

question: You want to enter a gap in highway traffic. You should:
options: a: Watch only the vehicles behind the gap.,b: Check traffic behind and beside you using your mirrors and by looking over your shoulder before merging.,c: Speed up and rely on other vehicles to make way for you.
note: To enter a gap in highway traffic safely, you must know what is happening both in front of you and behind you. Check your mirrors and look over your shoulder to check your blind spot before merging. Watching only the vehicles behind the gap or trying to force others to move by speeding up is unsafe.

question: When entering the interstate on a short entrance ramp where there is no acceleration lane, you should:
options: a: Immediately enter the far-right traffic lane on the interstate and speed up to match the flow of traffic.,b: Use the shoulder of the main road to get up to the speed of traffic.,c: Speed up and enter the interstate only after you have identified a gap in traffic.
note: On a short entrance ramp with no acceleration lane, you must use the ramp itself to build up speed, check traffic, and enter only when you have found a safe gap. Never use the shoulder as a makeshift acceleration lane, and do not force your way into traffic without a clear opening.

question: When merging onto the highway, find a gap in the closest lane, accelerate to match the flow of traffic, signal your intention, and:
options: a: Expect traffic to allow you to proceed into the lane,b: Merge carefully into the gap.,c: Wait for the lane to clear before merging.
note: When merging, you should identify a safe gap in the nearest lane, signal, accelerate to match the flow of traffic, and then merge smoothly into that gap. Do not assume other drivers will yield for you; it is your responsibility to merge only when it is safe.

question: Before merging onto the freeway, check traffic on the freeway by:
options: a: Using your rearview and side mirrors.,b: Using your rearview mirror.,c: Using your side mirror and looking over your shoulder.
note: Before merging onto a freeway, use your mirrors to check traffic and then look over your shoulder to check your blind spot in the lane you plan to enter. This combination of mirrors and a quick head check helps ensure there is no vehicle hidden alongside you before you merge.

question: As you approach your exit on the highway, when should you begin to slow down?
options: a: About halfway through the deceleration lane.,b: As you approach the deceleration lane.,c: Immediately upon entering the deceleration lane.
note: Use the deceleration lane to slow down, not the main travel lane. Maintain highway speed until you reach the deceleration lane, then reduce speed promptly and smoothly after you are in that lane so you do not disrupt through traffic.

question: You've been parked, signaling your intention to merge back into traffic, but have been waiting for a considerable period. Traffic volume is high. What should you do?
options: a: Continue waiting and yielding to traffic in the lane.,b: Slowly inch your vehicle into the traffic lane.,c: Drive on the shoulder until a gap in traffic appears.
note: When entering traffic from a parked or stopped position, you must yield to vehicles already moving in the lane. Wait until there is a large enough gap to signal, pull out, and accelerate to the speed of traffic. Do not force your way in or drive on the shoulder.

question: If the light is green but the intersection is blocked by other vehicles, how should you proceed?
options: a: Partially enter the intersection as allowed by traffic.,b: Wait and do not enter the intersection until your vehicle can get completely across.,c: Drive around the traffic on the shoulder to help ease the congestion.
note: A green light does not give you the right to block an intersection. You may only enter when there is enough space for your vehicle to clear completely. If traffic ahead is stopped and would trap you in the intersection, wait behind the stop line until you can get all the way through.

question: You must not pass another vehicle:
options: a: On a multi-lane one-way street,b: Where someone is likely to enter or cross the road,c: When a broken yellow line is on the left side of your lane
note: You must not pass where other road users are likely to enter or cross, such as at intersections, driveways, and crosswalks, because another vehicle, pedestrian, or cyclist may appear suddenly. Passing is allowed on multi‑lane one‑way streets and when a broken yellow line is on your side, as long as it is otherwise safe and legal.

question: When a vehicle approaching you initiates a left turn:
options: a: Maintain your speed and take your right of way,b: Honk your horn to warn the driver and maintain your speed,c: Slow or stop to prevent a collision
note: Even if you have the right‑of‑way, you must do whatever you reasonably can to avoid a collision. If an oncoming driver begins a left turn across your path, be prepared to slow or stop to prevent a crash, because right‑of‑way rules do not protect you from careless or mistaken drivers.

question: Passing another vehicle is permitted by driving on the unpaved shoulder of the road:
options: a: If the shoulder is wide enough to accommodate your vehicle,b: If the vehicle ahead of you is turning left,c: Under no circumstances
note: Driving on the unpaved shoulder to pass is unsafe and illegal in most situations. The shoulder is not designed for travel, may hide hazards, and other drivers will not expect a vehicle to pass there. You must stay on the paved, main‑traveled portion of the roadway when passing and only pass where it is legal and safe.

question: When you intend to pass a vehicle on the road, you must...
options: a: Wait until you can see the entire vehicle in your rearview mirror before merging back into your lane,b: Use your horn to alert the other driver of your intention to pass,c: Pass only if there is enough space in the lane ahead of the vehicle,d: None of the above
note: When passing, you must have enough clear space ahead to complete the pass and return safely, and you should not move back into your original lane until you can see the entire front of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror. This ensures you are not cutting too closely in front of the other driver and reduces the risk of a rear‑end collision.

question: Once you've passed a vehicle traveling in your direction, it's allowed to return to the right lane:
options: a: After about three seconds.,b: When you can no longer see the passed vehicle over your right shoulder.,c: When you can see the entire front of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror.
note: After passing, you should not return to the right lane until you can see the entire front of the vehicle you passed in your rearview mirror. This visual check confirms you have enough space ahead of the other vehicle and will not force that driver to brake suddenly when you move back into the lane.

question: When approaching the top of a hill, you should:
options: a: Speed up slightly.,b: Prepare to stop.,c: Maintain a steady, safe speed and be ready to slow or stop if needed.
note: As you approach the top of a hill, you should maintain a safe, steady speed and be prepared for hazards you cannot yet see, such as stopped traffic, slow vehicles, or pedestrians. You should not speed up, and you generally do not stop unless there is a specific hazard or traffic control requiring it. The key is to control your speed and be ready to react safely.

question: It is illegal to:
options: a: Pass another vehicle in any marked no passing zone.,b: Pass another vehicle over a railroad crossing.,c: Both of the above.
note: Passing is illegal both in a marked no‑passing zone and at or over a railroad crossing. No‑passing zones are marked with solid yellow lines or signs, and you must stay in your lane there. You also may not pass when approaching or on a railroad crossing, typically within about 100 feet, because trains cannot stop quickly and your view of the tracks or oncoming traffic may be limited.

question: When passing on a two-lane road, you should:
options: a: Sound your horn as you pass.,b: Flash your headlights as you pass.,c: Judge the distance to any oncoming vehicles.
note: Before passing on a two‑lane road, you must be sure there is enough clear distance ahead to complete the pass safely. That means carefully judging how far away oncoming vehicles are and how fast they are approaching. If you cannot clearly see enough open road ahead—such as near hills, curves, or other obstructions—you must not start to pass.

question: When passing another vehicle:
options: a: Pass the vehicle as slowly as possible.,b: Drive at the same speed as the vehicle you are passing.,c: Pass the vehicle as safely and as quickly as possible.
note: When you decide to pass, you should move into the passing lane, increase your speed within the legal limit, and complete the pass promptly. Lingering beside another vehicle is unsafe because it increases your time in the opposing lane and in the other driver’s blind spot. Passing should always be done as quickly as is safe and legal, never slowly or at the same speed as the vehicle you are overtaking.

question: Under what legal circumstances can a vehicle leave the roadway to overtake another?
options: a: If the vehicle ahead is turning left.,b: It is not legal under any conditions.,c: If there are two or more one-way lanes.
note: You must stay on the paved or main‑traveled portion of the roadway when passing. It is illegal to drive onto the shoulder, dirt, or any area off the roadway to overtake another vehicle, even if the vehicle ahead is turning left. Passing must be done only within marked lanes on the roadway where it is permitted and safe.

question: When being passed in a no-passing zone, you must:
options: a: Pull off the road.,b: Maintain your speed and position.,c: Slow down and let the other driver safely return to the drive lane.
note: When another driver begins to pass you, even in a no‑passing zone, you must not speed up or change your lane position. Maintain a steady speed and stay in your lane so the passing driver can judge distance and return safely. You may gently reduce speed if needed for safety, but you should not pull off the road or make sudden moves.

question: When passing, return to the right lane if:
options: a: You are one vehicle length ahead of the passed vehicle.,b: You can see both headlights of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror.,c: You are 50 feet ahead of the passed vehicle.
note: After passing another vehicle, do not move back into the right lane until you can see both of the passed vehicle’s headlights in your inside rearview mirror. This ensures you have enough space ahead of that vehicle and reduces the risk of cutting them off or forcing them to brake suddenly.

question: What's the correct way to parallel park?
options: a: Drive forward into the space without stopping.,b: Stop next to the vehicle behind the open space and then drive forward into the space.,c: Stop next to the vehicle in front of the open space and then back into the space.
note: For standard parallel parking, you first pull up alongside the vehicle in front of the open space, aligning your rear bumpers. Then you back slowly into the space while turning the wheel as directed, adjusting until you are parallel and centered in the space. You do not drive straight forward into a parallel space from the traffic lane.

question: Whould you do when parking your vehicle on a hill?
options: a: Turn your front wheels so the vehicle will roll into the curb or away from traffic if the brakes fail.,b: Make sure your vehicle is left in the 'neutral' position.,c: Make sure your vehicle is in the 'park' position or in gear.
note: When parking on a hill, always secure the vehicle so it cannot roll. Set the parking brake firmly and leave the transmission in Park (for automatic) or in a gear (for manual). In addition, you should turn the front wheels so that if the vehicle does roll, it will roll into the curb or away from traffic, not straight down the hill.

question: To back your vehicle safely, you must not…
options: a: Tap your horn before backing up,b: Check in front and behind your vehicle before you get in,c: Look over your right shoulder as you back up
note: You should never rely on tapping your horn as a primary safety step when backing. Safe backing requires checking both in front of and behind your vehicle before you get in, then looking over your right shoulder and using your mirrors while backing slowly. Sounding the horn is not a standard or required step in normal backing and can give a false sense of safety; the key is thorough observation, not noise.

question: During parallel parking:
options: a: Front wheels are turned toward the street,b: Vehicle is in line with other parked vehicles,c: Rear wheels are touching the curb
note: Parallel parking means your vehicle is parked parallel to the curb and in line with other parked vehicles. Your wheels should generally be straight and your car should not be sticking out into traffic or angled toward the street. The rear wheels should be close to, but not touching, the curb.

question: You are parking your vehicle on a hill. You should:
options: a: Leave the vehicle in neutral,b: Set the parking brake,c: Set the parking brake and leave the vehicle in park
note: When parking on a hill, you should always secure the vehicle by setting the parking brake and placing the transmission in park (or in gear for a manual). This prevents the vehicle from rolling if the brakes fail or if it is bumped. Never leave a parked vehicle on a hill in neutral.

question: Backing a vehicle is:
options: a: Always dangerous to do.,b: Dangerous if you have a helper.,c: Only dangerous in large vehicles.
note: Backing is always a potentially dangerous maneuver because your view is limited and other road users may be in your blind spots. Treat backing as a high‑risk action: check behind your vehicle before getting in, look over your right shoulder, use your mirrors, back slowly, and avoid unnecessary backing whenever possible. Even in small vehicles or with a helper, you must assume extra risk exists and use great caution.

question: If you're parallel parking downhill:
options: a: Turn your wheels sharply toward the side of the road.,b: Turn your wheels away from the side of the road.,c: Keep your wheels straight.
note: When you park facing downhill, turn your front wheels toward the curb or toward the side of the road. If the vehicle rolls, the front tire will contact the curb or shoulder and stop the car from rolling into traffic. Always set the parking brake as well.

question: When you are backing up your vehicle:
options: a: Look through the rear window while backing and check over your shoulder.,b: Press hard on the gas pedal.,c: Rely only on your rearview mirror.
note: When backing up, you should primarily look over your right shoulder through the rear window so you can clearly see the path behind you. Use your mirrors only as helpers, not your main view, and back up slowly using the brake, not the gas, so you can stop quickly if a person, vehicle, or object appears.

question: While parking your car parallel to the curb on a flat road:
options: a: Your front wheels must be turned toward the street.,b: Your wheels must be within 18 inches of the curb.,c: One of your rear wheels must touch the curb.
note: According to most state rules, when parallel parked your wheels must be close to the curb, typically within about 12–18 inches. This keeps your vehicle out of the traffic lane while avoiding contact with the curb.

question: When parking uphill on a two-way street without a curb, your front wheels should be...
options: a: Turn the front wheels to the left toward the center of the road.,b: Turn the front wheels to the right toward the side of the road.,c: Keep the front wheels parallel with the pavement.,d: Turn the wheels toward the curb (only applies when there is a curb).
note: On a hill with no curb, you always want the car to roll away from traffic if the brakes fail. When parking uphill on a two-way street without a curb, turn the front wheels to the right, toward the edge of the road. If the vehicle rolls, it will move off the roadway instead of into the traffic lane.

question: If you park facing uphill on a street with a curb, set the parking brake and:
options: a: Turn the front wheels toward the curb.,b: Turn the front wheels away from the curb.,c: Leave the front wheels straight.
note: When you park facing uphill with a curb, turn the front wheels away from the curb and let the vehicle roll back gently until the tire rests against the curb. If the brakes fail, the curb will stop the car from rolling into traffic.

question: When should your car's front wheels NOT be pointed directly forward?
options: a: When waiting to make a left turn at a traffic light.,b: When parked on a hill or sloping driveway.,c: When parked on the side of a level roadway where there is no curb.
note: Your front wheels should NOT be pointed straight ahead when you are parked on a hill or sloping driveway. On any slope, you must turn the wheels so that if the vehicle starts to roll, it will move away from traffic and not into the street. At a left turn at a traffic light, you should keep the wheels straight until you actually begin the turn, so you are not pushed into oncoming traffic if hit from behind.

question: To park downhill next to a curb, in which direction should you angle your front wheels?
options: a: Into the curb,b: Away from the curb,c: Parallel to the curb
note: When parking downhill next to a curb, turn your front wheels into the curb. If the brakes fail, the car will roll forward and the front tire will rest against the curb, stopping the vehicle from rolling into the traffic lane.

question: Who of the following can park at a blue curb?
options: a: Someone who is either picking up or dropping off passengers at this location.,b: A person who is disabled and has a special placard or vehicle license plate for disabled persons.,c: A person who will only be parked at the curb for less than 15 minutes.
note: A blue curb marks parking reserved for a person with a disability who has a valid disabled placard or special license plates, or for someone driving that person. Others may not park there, even briefly, unless they are transporting a person with a disability and displaying the proper placard or plates.

question: What curb color indicates no stopping or parking allowed?
options: a: Yellow.,b: Red.,c: White.
note: A red curb means you may not stop, stand, or park there at any time, except when required to obey a traffic control device or officer. Red is used to keep areas completely clear for safety or traffic flow.

question: You may not 'double park'
options: a: At any time,b: Except when making a delivery,c: Except while waiting in the vehicle
note: Double parking means stopping or parking alongside a vehicle already parked at the curb. This blocks traffic and can trap the parked vehicle, so it is not allowed at any time, even if you stay in the car or are making a delivery.

question: Parking is never permitted
options: a: In a tunnel,b: On the road side of a parked vehicle,c: All of the above
note: Parking is never allowed in a tunnel or on the road side of a parked vehicle (double parking). Tunnels are confined spaces where stopped vehicles create serious hazards, and double parking blocks traffic and visibility. Because both locations are prohibited, the correct choice is “All of the above.”

question: A blue-painted curb implies parking is:
options: a: Allowed for no longer than 15 minutes.,b: Only allowed when picking up or dropping off passengers.,c: For disabled persons with a special placard or plate.
note: A blue curb marks parking reserved for people with disabilities who display a valid disabled placard or license plate. Others may not park there, even briefly, because these spaces must remain available for drivers and passengers with mobility needs.

question: A red-painted curb indicates:
options: a: Loading zone.,b: The area is reserved for picking up or dropping off passengers.,c: No parking
note: A red curb means no stopping, standing, or parking at any time, except when required by traffic signals or officers. You may not use a red curb as a loading zone or for quick passenger drop‑off; the area must stay clear.

question: A white curb signifies:
